title: She Patrols Highways for the UP Police and Runs for India. Parul Chaudhary Just Smashed the 5000m National Record by Six Seconds.
excerpt: The 31-year-old DSP clocked 15:04.26 at a Continental Tour meet in Nice — smashing her own mark — but missed the CWG qualifying standard by 8 seconds.
body:
By day, she enforces the law on the highways of Moradabad. By night — or, in this case, under the evening lights of Nice — she chases national records.

Parul Chaudhary, India's premier distance runner and a serving Deputy Superintendent of Police in the Uttar Pradesh Police, broke the women's 5000m national record at the Meeting Nikaïa in France on Saturday, clocking 15:04.26 to shatter her own previous mark of 15:10.35 by more than six seconds.

The 31-year-old from Iklauta, a village near Meerut, finished second behind Ethiopia's Seniya Bereka (15:03.85) at the World Athletics Continental Tour Bronze event — her first 5000m race of the year and only her second competition of the 2026 season.

## Six Seconds Is a Lifetime

In distance running, shaving six seconds off a national record in a single race is seismic. For context, Chaudhary's previous mark had stood since May 2023, when she ran 15:10.35 at the Sound Running Track Fest in Walnut, California. The improvement in Nice suggests she is in the form of her life — even if the clock still was not quite fast enough.



> **"By night — or, in this case, under the evening lights of Nice — she chases national records."**


The Commonwealth Games qualifying standard in the 5000m is set at 14:56.60, a mark that only a handful of athletes in the world have breached this year. Chaudhary missed it by 7.66 seconds. But she had already secured her ticket to Glasgow in the 3000m steeplechase, having clocked 9:12.84 at the Shanghai Diamond League last month — comfortably clearing the qualifying mark of 9:27.41.

On Sunday, the AFI confirmed her place in India's 32-member squad for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, where she is expected to compete in the steeplechase. She is also targeting both the 5000m and steeplechase at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya in September.

## From Barefoot Teenager to DSP

Chaudhary's story is one of Indian sport's most quietly extraordinary. She grew up running barefoot in her village, competed in 800m races as a teenager, and gradually worked her way through 1500m and 3000m before discovering her twin specialities: the steeplechase and the 5000m.

A job with the Western Railway brought her to Mumbai in 2015. Her rise through the ranks accelerated at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, where she won gold in the 5000m and added a steeplechase medal to her collection. By January 2024, she had been appointed Deputy Superintendent of Police in Moradabad — a prestigious government posting that she balances alongside a relentless international competition schedule.

At the Paris Olympics, she narrowly missed the 5000m final, finishing 24th overall with a time of 15:10.68, agonisingly close to her own national record. Her steeplechase result was similarly competitive but fell short of the final.

## Where She Stands Globally

The world-leading time in the 5000m this year is 14:18.76 — more than 45 seconds faster than Chaudhary's record. Over 60 athletes worldwide have run under 15 minutes in 2026. India's distance runners still have a significant gap to close against the East African powerhouses who dominate the event.

But the trajectory is undeniable. Chaudhary joins Avinash Sable — the men's steeplechase national record-holder who won a historic silver at the 2022 Commonwealth Games — in pushing Indian distance running into conversations it was never part of a decade ago.

For the diaspora, her dual life as a police officer and a world-class athlete is a story that resonates deeply. In a country where sport beyond cricket often struggles for recognition and financial support, Chaudhary's path from Meerut to Nice is a reminder that India's next great athletic chapter is being written by people who hold day jobs.
